summary: Built in 1823 at Ocracoke Inlet and lit in 1824, the light had resident keepers until 1954; the Park Service now shares the station with the Coast Guard.

lens.note: Fourth-order Fresnel lens installed 1854, replacing reflectors (NPS). Removed in the Civil War and reinstalled 1863 or 1864 (see conflicts).

structures.note: About 75 feet tall (NPS). Walls 5 feet thick at the base, tapering to 2 feet.
One-story brick house of three rooms, 16-inch walls (NRHP); second story 1897 and a frame section 1928-29 (NRHP, NPS).

access.note: Not open for climbing (narrow spaces, small doors, ladders). Base open for limited hours in summer; the Ocracoke Discovery Center has current times.

facts.agency: National Park Service (station; tower title since 1999). The U.S. Coast Guard still owns and operates the light and lens.

events.note: Congress authorizes $20,000 for a lighthouse on Ocracoke Island (7 May 1822); two acres bought for $50 from Jacob Gaskill
Tower and keeper's quarters built; contract signed 20 June 1823 with builder Noah Porter; cost $11,359.35; completed by December 1823
First lit 15 August 1824 according to correspondence cited by NPS. The NRHP gives construction in 1823; the USLHS place record gives 1828.
Fourth-order Fresnel lens replaces the reflector apparatus (NPS; NRHP)
Franklin lamps replace the valve lamps (NRHP)
Fresnel lens removed during the Civil War (NRHP). NPS says Confederate troops dismantled it early in the war.
Tower refitted and light re-exhibited (NRHP). NPS dates the reinstallation by Union forces to 1864.
Dwelling roof removed and a full story added, giving three rooms (Board report for fiscal 1896). The NRHP dates the same work to 1897.
Second story added to the original quarters (NRHP; NPS)
New fourth-order lamps supplied; repairs (NRHP)
Hurricane of 2-3 September 1913 damages the light station (Board report). Keeper Wesley Austin gives shelter to island residents.
Putnam says 27 people took refuge in the light-tower after their dwellings were destroyed in the September 1913 storm (secondary account)
Light electrified by generator (NPS). NRHP says electric bulbs replaced oil vapor lamps in 1938.
Another section added to the quarters (NPS; NRHP 1928-29)
1944 hurricane: stairway removed and replaced with ladders; coal shed severely damaged and collapsed (NRHP)
Wooden stairs replaced with steel spiral stairway (NRHP)
Fully automated; last resident keeper leaves (NPS)
Quarters transferred to the National Park Service under a special use permit (NRHP). NPS says the Coast Guard agreed in 1955 to let the Park Service use them.
Listed on the National Register of Historic Places (NRHP 77000110)
Coast Guard transfers title of the lighthouse and about two acres to the National Park Service (7 June 1999); Coast Guard still owns and operates the light and lens (NPS)
Hurricane Dorian floods the keepers' quarters with 18 inches of water (NPS)

corrections.current: 1798 built (under the station record's built events)
corrections.proposed: remove from this station; it describes the wooden tower on Shell Castle Island
corrections.why: NPS: the wooden pyramid tower on Shell Castle Island was completed in 1798; the present tower dates from 1823.
NPS cites correspondence for a first lighting on 15 August 1824. The 1823 date is the construction date in the NRHP nomination.
NPS gives the tower as about 75 feet (22.9 m). The 25.9 m figure appears to belong to the Shell Castle or another tower.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The record gives 1823 (first lit), 1824 (built, Rowlett) and 1828 (USLHS established). NPS gives 15 August 1824 from correspondence, and the NRHP gives 1823 for construction. The story follows NPS for the first lighting and gives the NRHP date as the construction date.

resolved_conflicts.field: lens relighting after the Civil War
resolved_conflicts.explanation: NRHP says the light was re-exhibited by 1863; NPS says Union forces reinstalled the lens in 1864. Not resolved; both are given in the story.
NPS says 1929 (generator); NRHP says 1938 (electric bulbs replaced oil vapor lamps). Not resolved.

resolved_conflicts.field: quarters transfer to the Park Service
resolved_conflicts.explanation: NRHP says 1957 under a special use permit; NPS says the Coast Guard agreed to the use in 1955. Both are given.
The Board's report for fiscal 1896 describes the roof work, and the NRHP dates it to 1897. Both are given.

notes_for_editor: NPS and NRHP agree on the 1823 construction, the $11,359 cost, the 1854 lens and the 1954 automation, which are the core facts. The first lighting date, the Civil War relighting, the electrification year and the quarters transfer are disputed between them, and the story says so. The NRHP prints the Shell Castle lighthouse's completion year as '1700', most likely a misprint for 1798 (NPS gives 1798); the story follows NPS and does not use the NRHP's date. The station record's '1798 built' event belongs to Shell Castle. Burrus: the Board's 1924-1929 index has 'Burrus, J.M., keeper Bluff Shoal' and the 1927 Bulletin lists 'J. M. Burrus, Bluff Shoal, N.C.' The sources do not connect that man with Joe Burrus of Ocracoke, so the story does not link them. Crawford R. Austin: the 1912-1917 Board index lists an 'Austin, Crawford, R., asst keeper Harbor Island Bar, rescue'; the roster lists a Crawford R. Austin as first assistant at Ocracoke, 1929-1940. Not linked; editor to decide. Wesley Austin's efficiency flag: the index gives the page (275) but not the year, so no event year is given. The 1913 storm: the Board's report dates it 2-3 September; Putnam's account (27 people in the tower) and the Board's (Austin's shelter, residents 'driven from their homes by the high tides') differ in cause and number, and the story keeps both. No newspaper search was made for this station. The loc.gov service returned HTTP 520 errors during this session. The NRHP's Burrus quotation is from a 1951 Coastland Times article (Alice Rondthaler), quoted in the nomination; no independent copy was read. Photos not searched. Checker (2026-10-22): the 1927 Bulletin page image (PDF p. 6, printed p. 174) reads 'from the fifth district, J. M. Burrus, Bluff Shoal, N. C.', which supplies the North Carolina state given in the story; the 1924-1929 index entry gives no state.
